description: ChronoStrider is a multidisciplinary team from Bangladesh tackling NASA's challenge to build health monitoring software for astronauts, turning biometric data into clear, life-saving insight. We bring engineering, data science, UI/UX, product, and storytelling. Join us if you're passionate about space and health tech and skilled in software, web development, hardware, coding, or arts & multimedia.
summary:
ASTRA is an onboard health monitoring software that lets astronauts spot and act on health problems without waiting for Earth. It grades every vital sign against NASA-STD-3001 limits and each astronaut's own baseline, maps eight body systems in 3D, and guides emergency protocols offline.

Its core is Crew Watch, an on-board agent that acts without being asked. When two crew report the same headache, it checks each person's vitals, then the cabin air, finds the shared cause (CO2 above the 3.0 mmHg limit), tells the crew to fix the scrubber, and reports to Earth, in 56 milliseconds.

Every limit, dose, and delay comes from real NASA data, stored on board: JPL Horizons Earth-Mars light time, including the 2028 solar conjunction; NASA OSDR ISS cabin CO2 and radiation (RR-7); 336 Inspiration4 blood values (OSD-575); the DONKI October 2021 solar storm as a shelter alert; NASA-STD-3001 Vol 1 & 2 and OCHMO CO2 limits. All 17 NASA HRP risks are mapped to ASTRA's features.

Near Mars, a question to Earth and back takes up to 44 minutes. Following NASA's goal of Earth-independent medical care, ASTRA makes every crew, from Mars to remote clinics on Earth, its own first responder.
details:
ASTRA: Astronaut Self-Triage & Readiness Assistant

On the International Space Station, a doctor is one call away. Near Mars, a question to Earth and back takes up to 44 minutes, and when the Sun passes between the planets, the link is lost for weeks. Evacuation is not an option. NASA calls the answer Earth-independent medical operations: the crew has to be its own first responder, and not every astronaut is a doctor.

ASTRA is a working prototype of that capability. It is health monitoring software that runs entirely on board. It helps every astronaut gather health indicators, evaluate them against NASA limits and their own body, and act with clear guidance, all without waiting for Earth.

What ASTRA does

Gather. ASTRA tracks 14 health indicators plus a daily symptom check: heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, breathing rate, temperature, blood glucose, hydration, body mass, nutrition, sleep, mood, reaction time (tap test), vision (Amsler grid, for spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome) and exercise. A daily routine prompts each check at the right time, and every measurement explains how to take it and why it matters in space.

Evaluate. A deterministic, tested rules engine grades every reading Nominal, Watch or Act against NASA-STD-3001 limits and the astronaut's own baseline. A heart rate that is normal for most people but high for *you* becomes Watch. The engine also knows each person's medical history, the context of a reading (rest, after exercise, after an EVA), and joins related readings into one finding instead of five alarms: sleep debt, early infection, blood-pressure drift, possible SANS signs, deconditioning, kidney-stone risk and weight loss.

Act. Every result comes with plain-language guidance and an escalation ladder: self-care, then the Crew Medical Officer, then the flight surgeons on Earth. Messages to Earth are delay-aware, with live countdowns based on the real signal delay. Four step-by-step emergency protocols, including CPR in microgravity, run fully offline.

Every feature, at a glance

Monitoring and measurement

14 health indicators plus a daily symptom check, each with a guided wizard: Prepare, Why it matters in space, Measure, Result. Inputs include a cuff reading, a 3-trial reaction-time tap test, an Amsler grid for vision and a 5-face mood picker. The symptom check has 14 symptoms; the 4 red-flag ones send the crew straight to the emergency protocol.

Readings in context: heart rate, blood pressure and breathing are graded for rest, waking, after exercise or after an EVA. Post-exertion readings use recovery ranges, never pollute the baseline, and prompt a 30-minute recheck.

- Daily routine: 8 timed checks a day plus 2 weekly ones, with due and overdue states. Surface missions add a post-EVA check.

- Personal baselines: every reading is compared with the astronaut's own history (z-score), not only a population range.

- Escalation ladder: the Crew Medical Officer is involved for any Act, or a Watch lasting 3+ days; flight surgeons for red flags or an Act lasting 2+ days.

- Insights: related readings join into one finding (sleep debt, early infection, blood-pressure drift, possible SANS signs, deconditioning, kidney-stone risk, weight loss) instead of five separate alarms.

- Today dashboard: a Health Orbit ring of every indicator by status, what needs attention, the next checks, the EVA status, radiation dose and cabin air in one view.

- Trends: 7, 14 and 30-day charts with status zones and the personal baseline, a second indicator to compare, and hover or keyboard inspection.

- 3D body map: eight body systems coloured by status, always with a text label. The heart beats at the astronaut's measured heart rate and the lungs breathe at their measured breathing rate. Muscle and skeletal views, organ layers, and a 2D fallback when 3D is unavailable.

- Crew profiles: each past diagnosis names the indicators it makes likely to drift and why, and the app watches those more closely.

Crew, ship and Earth

- Crew roster: every crew member ranked by urgency, with overall status, EVA go / caution / no-go and today's checks. Any screen can be viewed as any crewmate.

- Ship Sense: when two or more crew report the same symptom, it checks the habitat before treating separate patients.

- Crew Watch agent: acts on its own (described below).

- Attention queue: one list of everything open, by person and habitat. Anyone can acknowledge; only the Crew Medical Officer can resolve, and only with a note.

- Earth link: store-and-forward messages to flight surgeons with live delay countdowns, the next comm window and the real delay from JPL Horizons.

- Solar conjunction: a 30-day warning before the Sun blocks the Earth–Mars link, then blackout mode, with ASTRA guiding the crew through it.

Emergencies

- Four step-by-step protocols that run fully offline, including CPR in microgravity, with a running timer, a patient picker and branching tracks.

- Drill mode for practice, and a run that survives a page reload, so an emergency is never lost mid-protocol. The finished timeline is sent to Earth.

- Focus mode: during an emergency only emergency and timer sounds can play.

- Even with the engine down, the four protocols still open from a static file.

Environment and radiation

- Five mission environments (Mars transit, space station, lunar rover, lunar base, Mars base) that change gravity, signal delay, radiation dose rate, routine and advice.

- Radiation tracking: dose against the 600 mSv NASA career limit, using Curiosity RAD dose rates (1.84 mSv/day in transit, 0.64 mSv/day on Mars).

- Solar storm replay: the real October 2021 event from NASA DONKI, with a countdown to reach the shelter.

- Cabin air: real ISS CO₂ telemetry against NASA's one-hour and seven-day limits.

Exercise countermeasures

- A weekly plan modelled on NASA's SPRINT study: resistance training 3 days a week and aerobic training 3 days a week, with intervals above 90% of maximum heart rate.

- 8 exercises on 7 real devices, mapped per location: ARED, the T2 treadmill and the CEVIS cycle on the station, a compact flywheel in transit where there is no room for them.

- Personal adjustments, each day's plan changes with the person's medical history (a repaired knee, raised blood pressure, a past kidney stone) and today's readings (a fever means a light session, short sleep swaps intervals for steady work), and every change says why.

- Guided sessions: an animated astronaut demonstrates each exercise, with short NASA and JAXA video clips.

AI

- AI assistant (NVIDIA Nemotron): a chat on every page that retrieves only the relevant live data (crew status, readings, history, alerts, today's exercise, the page you are on), recognises emergencies and follows the escalation ladder. Readings in its answers render as live cards from the data itself, so the numbers never come from the model. It never raises or clears an alert, and when the link is down, rule-based answers reply instead. Suggested questions change with each page.

- Notifications: one log of your open alerts, the crew's Act alerts and replies from Earth.

Motivation: Honest Orbit

- XP for doing the checks, never for the numbers: on-time bonuses, streak days, a Full orbit bonus when every check of the day is done, and a Welcome back bonus after a missed day.

- Health-positive actions earn more: re-measuring after an alert, checking on a crewmate's alert and running an emergency drill.

- Personal quests drawn from each person's own medical history, 6 levels, 13 badges, and forgiving streaks with shields and a momentum guard for hard weeks.

- Mission chapters that follow the 180-day mission, with weekly cooperative crew operations.

- One crew, one goal: no leaderboard; the crew competes with its own last week. Crew rewards (a playlist, movie night, longer family calls) unlock together once the Commander approves them.

Smart alert sounds

- Ranked alarm sounds based on IEC 60601-1-8 and NASA caution-and-warning practice: emergency, then Act, then Watch.

- Each alert sounds once, and an open Act alert reminds at most twice, so alarms never become noise. Settings offer All, Alerts only or Off, with volume.

Learn and reference

- Health library: NASA's five hazards (radiation, isolation, distance, gravity, hostile environment), every body system and every indicator in plain words.

- Challenge resources: all 17 NASA HRP risks mapped to what ASTRA does, 13 ongoing HRP studies matched to their on-board counterpart, and the CSA resources.

- Inspiration4 analysis: 12 analytes, 4 crew, 336 values, graded by ASTRA's lab rule. A NASA data page lists every source and 49 cited documents; in the app, every number links to the document behind it.

Built for real crews

- Works fully offline; data stays on board, and the only outbound call is the optional AI assistant.

- Colour is always paired with text; it is keyboard-accessible and covered by automated accessibility tests.

- Light and dark themes.


Crew Watch: the on-board agent

Crew Watch is what makes ASTRA different. Most health apps watch one person at a time. Crew Watch watches the crew and the ship together, and it acts without being asked.

When two crew members report the same symptom, it runs four steps:

1. Sense: two crew logged a headache in the last 24 hours.

2. Check: each person's vitals against their own baseline, then the cabin air.

3. Decide: with ASTRA's rules, it finds a shared cause, cabin CO₂ above NASA's 3.0 mmHg one-hour limit, instead of treating two separate patients.

4. Act: it tells the crew to check the CO₂ scrubber and increase airflow, then sends a report to the flight surgeons, stamped with when Earth will read it.

In our recorded run, all seven steps took 56 milliseconds, on board, with no network. The report then needed 19 minutes 31 seconds to reach Earth. Every step is logged, so the crew and Earth can see exactly why ASTRA decided what it did.

How it works

ASTRA has two parts. ASTRA Core is a Python engine that owns every medical rule, baseline, insight, escalation and the Crew Watch agent, with a SQLite store. The crew app is a Next.js web app for a laptop or tablet. The app never calls the engine from the browser; every call happens server-side, so the explanation a crew member reads always matches the logic that classified their reading.

Rules decide, AI explains. Every alert comes from the tested rules engine, so every alert is explainable and repeatable. On top of it, an AI assistant built on NVIDIA Nemotron answers crew questions using only that crew's own readings, history and alerts. It never raises or clears an alert, and when the link is down the rules engine answers instead.

Offline by design. All NASA data was downloaded ahead of time and stored on board as small fixture files with a manifest, so ASTRA Core never makes a network call in flight.


Real NASA data on board

Every threshold, dose and delay comes from a real NASA source, and in the app every number links to the document behind it.

- JPL Horizons: real Earth–Mars light time and Sun–Mars angle for 541 days, including the 2028 solar conjunction. It drives the signal delay, the comms countdowns and the blackout warning.

- NASA OSDR, Environmental Data Application (Rodent Research-7): real ISS cabin CO₂, temperature, humidity and crew radiation dose.

- NASA OSDR, Inspiration4 (OSD-575, OSD-569): 336 real blood and urine values from four civilian astronauts, used to test ASTRA's lab rules. ASTRA flags 17 of them (9 at Act), including low potassium (3.0 mmol/L) the day after landing.

- NASA DONKI: the real 28 October 2021 X1.0 solar flare and particle event, replayed as a radiation-shelter alert.

- Curiosity MSL/RAD: measured doses of 1.84 mSv/day in transit and 0.64 mSv/day on Mars.

- NASA-STD-3001 Volumes 1 & 2: the 600 mSv career limit, the 3.0 mmHg one-hour CO₂ limit and vital-sign ranges.

- NASA OCHMO-TB-004: the 2.5 mmHg seven-day CO₂ threshold and its link to headaches.

- NASA Human Research Program: all 17 HRP risks are mapped to what ASTRA does (11 measured, 4 supported, 2 gaps named honestly), and 13 ongoing HRP studies are matched to their on-board counterpart.



Benefits

- For each astronaut: clear, personal answers in seconds instead of a 40-minute wait, with guidance a non-doctor can follow.

- For the Crew Medical Officer: one crew view, ranked by urgency, with the shared causes already found.

- For flight surgeons: structured, evidence-backed reports instead of raw data, delivered through the delay.

- For mission safety: problems are caught early, alarms stay meaningful, and care continues through blackouts.

- For people on Earth: the same offline, explainable approach works where help is far away. 4.6 billion people lack essential health services (WHO & World Bank, 2025).

What we hope to achieve

We want every crew, from Mars to remote clinics on Earth, to be its own first responder. Our next steps:

1. Live sensors: connect wearable vitals and live cabin (ECLSS) feeds in place of manual entry and today's cabin model.

2. An on-board AI model: run the assistant locally so it works with no link at all.

3. Field pilots: test ASTRA in a Mars-analog mission and in offline clinics at home in Bangladesh.

Tools and technologies

ASTRA Core: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, SQLite; pytest (150 engine tests) and Ruff; managed with uv.

Crew app: TypeScript, Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei for the 3D body map, hand-built SVG charts, Motion for animation and Lucide icons.

Quality: Playwright end-to-end tests, including accessibility checks; oxlint.

AI: NVIDIA Nemotron through NVIDIA NIM, with a rules-only fallback.

NASA data pipeline: standard-library Python downloaders for JPL Horizons, NASA OSDR and DONKI, with a manifest recording where each file came from and how it was cleaned.

Hardware: none beyond a standard laptop or tablet; the whole system runs locally and offline.

Demo video: Remotion (React video), real screen recordings of the prototype, NASA public footage.

What we considered

Safety and honesty: ASTRA is a decision-support prototype, not a medical device. The crew and mission (MERIDIAN-1) are fictional; the environment data is real NASA data, and every threshold cites its source.

Trust: deterministic rules make every alert explainable and repeatable. The AI only explains, from the crew's own data.

Human factors: colour is always paired with text, alarms are ranked to prevent alarm fatigue, instructions are written for non-experts, and gamification never rewards health numbers or ranks people.

Privacy: data stays on board, and the AI sees only the records of the crew member asking.
